questions.q: What does the summary say our desire to be “somebody” really comes from?
a: A wish to feel respected and loved by others
A natural appetite for material goods
A competitive instinct shared with animals
A need to control the people around us
questions.why: Lesson 1 says status-seeking is really about wanting to matter to someone and to be loved.

questions.q: Why does status seeking create so much stress?
a: It makes us base our identity on other people’s opinions
It requires more money than most people can earn
It forces us to work longer hours than we should
It turns friends into competitors for the same job
questions.why: Lesson 1 says that without a sense of your own worth, you end up measuring yourself by what others think.

questions.q: Why didn’t the fall of the hereditary class system reduce status anxiety?
a: Once improvement became possible, people felt restless for more
People simply stopped comparing themselves to neighbors
Equality made everyone content with what they had
New laws fixed the incomes of every citizen
questions.why: Lesson 2 says attainable affluence turned into an expectation, so falling short produced constant unease.

questions.q: When do we decide that what we have is enough, according to the summary?
a: Only when we see how much others have
When our basic needs are comfortably met
When we have saved a fixed sum of money
When our parents approve of our choices
questions.why: Lesson 2 says we measure sufficiency against our neighbors, so enough only feels like enough if it is more than theirs.

questions.q: What did Diogenes show when he asked Alexander the Great to move?
a: That he cared nothing for social status
That he wanted a reward from the king
That he feared the king’s power
That he was seeking a position at court
questions.why: Lesson 3 uses the story to show a philosopher indifferent to rank, and Alexander’s amused admiration.
